george-mitchell-live-oak-1895-07.A3:
GEORGE MITCHELL HANGED.
He Was the Second to Hang for a Murder.
Another Will Probably Follow.
LIVE OAK, FLA., Aug. 1.—George Mitchell (colored) was hanged here today in the presence of a large crowd for complicity in the murder and robbery of Alfred Ryberg, a white man. Mitchell to the last protested his innocence. His last words were:

"Everybody meet me in heaven. I feel that my soul is saved, and I want to see my friends in glory. I die without hard feelings against any one."

Mitchell is the second man to hang for Ryberg's murder, Henry Brown having been executed for the same crime July 17th. Brown, Mitchell, and Stevens were convicted and sentenced to death for the crime, but the two latter were respited. The respite caused such indignation that a mob attempted to storm the jail and lynch Mitchell and Stevens a few days ago.

The Governor decided to let the law take its course in the case of Mitchell, but is still considering Stevens' appeal for clemency. It is believed that Stevens will be allowed to hang, as the chances are that he would be lynched if clemency were extended.

When Brown was hanged he swore on the scaffold that he alone killed Ryberg, and that Mitchell and Stevens were innocent.
george-mitchell-live-oak-1895-07.A4:
A HANGING AT LIVE OAK.
The Second of the Ryeburg Murderers on the Gallows.
Live Oak, Fla., Aug. 1.—On the same gallows from which Henry Brown was hanged on July 17. George Mitchell, a second of the Ryeburg murderers, was executed today. The execution was public, about 1,000 spectators being present. Mitchell was brought out at 11 a. m., and after a religious service, he spent over an hour in a religious talk, protesting his innocence. Mitchell did not have a bad face and some of the spectators think he may have been innocent. He died without a struggle.

For many weeks this county has been on the verge of a lynching, owing to the general impression that the execution of Brown, Mitchell and Stevens, the murderers of Alfred Ryeburg, would not take place. This impression was probably deeper-seated because the evidence against these negroes was circumstantial and owing to the frequent long delays and commutations that serve to defeat justice.

But the evidence, though circumstantial, was strong. Ryeburg in his dying statement said that the three train hands inflicted the wounds from which he was dying, and Ryeburg had been on this train, which was a freight train, for several hours and had every opportunity to know the train hands and undoubtedly did know them. He said positively there were three negroes and all the evidence proved that these were the only three negroes on board.

Subsequently Brown acknowledged his guilt and Stevens said Brown and Mitchell did the killing, while he stood by and saw it done.

So when Brown, in his talk on the gallowss, said he alone killed Ryeburg, everybody believed Brown died with a lie in his mouth, and especially so since Brown had made several contradictory affidavits previously.

Mitchell was a young negro, yet in his 20's; he claimed to be a member of a Baptist church at Thomasville, Ga., and that he had been a Christian ever since he joined the church.

Rev. George P. McKinney was his spiritual adviser and gave him constant attention till the execution.

There is no further fear of a lynching, as everybody believes that Stevens, the third man, will hang soon.
george-mitchell-live-oak-1895-07.A5:
Publicly Executed.
LIVE OAK, Fla., Aug. 2.—George Mitchell was hanged yesterday in the presence of a large crowd of men, women and children of all colors. He made a long harangue on the gallows, protesting his innocence. Mitchell was one of three men who beat to death Alfred Byborg, robbing him of 25 cents.

HANGMAN'S DAY.
Two Colored Men Executed in the Coke Regions of Pennsylvania.
Two Colored Men Executed in the Coke Regions of Pennsylvania.

John Goode and William Freeman, colored, were hanged in the court yard at Greensburg, Penn. The men walked to the scaffold with firm steps at 10.08 o'clock. The trap was sprung immediately. Death was caused by strangulation. The crime for which Goode was executed was for the killing of Max Slaughter, a fellow worker, over a game of craps. Freeman shot and killed his sweetheart, Gertie A. Timberlake, on July 15, 1894, because she refused to give him money. About 200 persons witnessed the executions.

At Live Oak, Fla., Henry Brown, colored, was hanged for the murder of Ed Ryberg, a white man, on March 27. Brown stated that he alone killed Ryberg, and that George Mitchell and Mike Stevens, who were tried and convicted with him, are innocent. There was talk of lynching Mitchell and Stevens. Brown confessed that he had murdered seven men, all for robbery.

At Washington James L. Travers, a colored man, was hanged at the District jail at 11.36 o'clock a. m. for the murder of his sweetheart, Lena Gross, last November.

george-mitchell-live-oak-1895-07.A12:
HANGING OF MIKE STEVENS.
The Third Man Executed for Alfred Ryberg's Murder.
Live Oak, Fla., Sept. 18.—At 11:45 o'clock this morning the drop fell and Mike Stevens, the third of the Ryburg murderers, was pronounced dead a few minutes later by the doctors present.

Stevens died protesting his innocence and asserting that he was going to heaven. He refused to be questioned by Capt. Jolly, to whom he had made a partial confession at the time of his arrest.

Only a small crowd was present at the execution, although it was public. Money was raised by passing the hat around to send the body to McIntosh, Ga., for burial.

Very noticeable in the crowd was a number of white women with little babies in their arms. The general impression is that such exhibitions as public hanging do not have a very good effect on the tougher element of any community, and it is a very generally expressed desire that Live Oak won't have to be called upon to witness any more such exhibitions soon.
